etymology.text: From Middle High German reise, reis, from Old High German reisa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu.

funFacts: Gute Reise! is the standard farewell to someone setting off; for a trip by car people also say Gute Fahrt!
pitfalls: eine Reise machen – the usual verb is machen, not *nehmen.
Do not confuse die Reise (trip) and der Reis (rice).
subtleties: reisen is the verb (to travel); die Reise is the noun: Ich reise gern – Die Reise war schön.
Many compounds: die Urlaubsreise, die Geschäftsreise (business trip), das Reisebüro (travel agency), der Reisepass.

etymology.text: From Buch (“book”) + -en, probably modelled on English to book.

funFacts: The verb comes from das Buch (to enter in a book); the travel meaning probably followed English to book.
pitfalls: buchen is regular: buchte, gebucht.
A table in a restaurant is usually reserviert, not gebucht.
subtleties: buchen is also the accountant’s verb: to enter in the books (einen Betrag buchen).
ausgebucht = fully booked; die Buchung = the booking.

inseparable.none: no prefix; the participle has no ge- because the verb ends in -ieren

etymology.text: From French réserver, from Latin reservāre (“to keep back”); -ieren is the usual German ending of borrowed verbs.

funFacts: Every verb in -ieren is weak and has no ge-: reservieren, telefonieren, studieren – reserviert, telefoniert, studiert.
pitfalls: Verbs in -ieren take no ge- in the participle: reserviert, not *gereserviert.
The stress is on -ie-: reser-VIE-ren.
subtleties: die Reservierung = the reservation; reserviert also means reserved, aloof (of a person).

etymology.text: Compound of Reise (“travel”) + Pass (“passport”); Pass is a shortening of Early New High German paßport, borrowed from French passeport.

funFacts: Pass (passport) comes from French passeport – the paper to pass the port (gate).
pitfalls: der Reisepass – masculine like der Pass; plural die Reisepässe.
Spelled with ss (short a); the old spelling was Reisepaß.
subtleties: In speech most people say der Pass: Hast du deinen Pass dabei?
Germans travel inside much of Europe with the Personalausweis (ID card) and use the Reisepass for other countries.

etymology.text: Back-formation from Ausländer (“foreigner”), from Middle High German ūzlender; by surface analysis aus + Land. Compare English outland.

funFacts: The genitive -s appears in compounds: der Auslandsaufenthalt, die Auslandsreise.
pitfalls: German uses a noun with a preposition where other languages have an adverb: im Ausland (abroad, where?), ins Ausland (abroad, where to?), aus dem Ausland (from abroad).
das Ausland is neuter, like das Land; it has no plural.
subtleties: The opposite is das Inland (home country): im In- und Ausland (at home and abroad).
der Ausländer / die Ausländerin = foreigner; the word can sound distancing, so people often say Menschen aus dem Ausland.

etymology.text: From Middle High German besuochen (“to seek, use, visit, investigate”), from Old High German bisuohhen, by surface analysis be- + suchen (“to seek”). Cognate with Dutch bezoeken, Swedish besöka, English beseech.

pitfalls: besuchen takes a direct object (accusative): Ich besuche dich – not *Ich besuche zu dir.
be- is inseparable: the participle is besucht, without ge-.
subtleties: besuchen also means to attend: eine Schule besuchen, einen Kurs besuchen.
der Besuch is the visit and the visitors: Wir haben Besuch (we have guests).

etymology.text: From Reise (“journey”) + Leiter (“leader”); Leiter is from Middle High German leitære, Old High German leitāri, equivalent to leiten (“to lead”) + -er.

funFacts: der Leiter (leader) and die Leiter (ladder) are two different words that only look alike – the article tells them apart.
pitfalls: der Reiseführer is usually the guidebook (a book), though it can also mean a guide; der Reiseleiter is always a person.
Do not confuse der Leiter (leader, manager) with die Leiter (ladder).
subtleties: A Reiseleiter travels with the group and organises; a Stadtführer or Gästeführer shows one town.
Plural without ending: die Reiseleiter; dative plural den Reiseleitern.

etymology.text: From nächste (“next”, the superlative of nah “near”) + Woche (“week”); the phrase is an accusative of time.

funFacts: The opposite is letzte Woche (last week); diese Woche is this week.
pitfalls: No preposition: nächste Woche (accusative of time), not *in nächste Woche.
Masculine and neuter nouns change the ending: nächsten Monat, nächstes Jahr – nächste Woche (feminine).
subtleties: After bis the phrase stays the same: Bis nächste Woche! (See you next week!).
nächste is the superlative of nah (near): the nearest week is the next one.

etymology.text: From nächstes (“next”, the superlative of nah “near”, neuter accusative) + Jahr (“year”); an accusative of time.

funFacts: letztes Jahr (last year) and dieses Jahr (this year) follow the same pattern.
pitfalls: nächstes Jahr ends in -es because das Jahr is neuter and there is no article: not *nächste Jahr.
No preposition: nächstes Jahr, not *in nächstes Jahr.
subtleties: In the genitive (written style): Anfang nächsten Jahres.
The future is often said with the present: Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Spanien.

lexemes.role: Taught here as the auxiliary of the future (werden + infinitive at the end of the clause); its own meaning “to become” is not a lesson concept yet.

governs.note: predicative nominative or an adjective: Er wird Lehrer. Es wird kalt.

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Change and what is to come: it gets dark, she becomes a doctor, we will see.

senses.def: to become, to get, to grow (a change of state): Es wird kalt.
auxiliary of the future: werden + infinitive (Ich werde morgen kommen)

examples.text: Es wird schon dunkel.
examples.tr: It’s already getting dark.

examples.text: Sie wird Ärztin.

examples.text: Ich werde nächstes Jahr in Berlin studieren.

examples.text: Wir werden sehen.
examples.tr: We’ll see.

examples.text: Morgen wird es regnen.
examples.tr: It will rain tomorrow.

synonyms.nuance: to turn into, to transform (completely)

etymology.text: From Middle High German wërden, from Old High German wërdan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną. Cognate with Dutch worden, obsolete English worth (“to become”), and Latin vertō (“to turn”). The use as a future auxiliary is a Middle High German innovation.

funFacts: The future with werden is younger than the language itself: it became common only in Middle High German; before, the present did the job – and it still often does.
pitfalls: werden is not “want”: Ich will kommen = I want to come; Ich werde kommen = I will come.
bekommen is a false friend: it means to get, to receive – not to become (that is werden).
du wirst, er wird – the vowel changes and the d of the stem disappears in du wirst; ihr werdet.
With the future the infinitive goes to the very end: Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahren.
subtleties: As a full verb it takes sein in the perfect: Er ist Lehrer geworden; as the passive auxiliary the participle is worden (Das Haus ist gebaut worden).
werden + infinitive can also express a guess about the present: Er wird schon zu Hause sein (he’s probably at home by now).
Präteritum wurde; the old form ward appears in literature.
